einzeiler: How photo-matching and authentication transformed game-worn sports memorabilia.
kurzfassung: Barry Meisel discusses the founding of MeiGray and the forensic process of photo-matching game-worn sports memorabilia. He examines high-profile sales, including a Michael Jordan Finals jersey, and addresses counterfeit items in the collecting market. The conversation also covers game-worn relic cards and the future growth of authenticated sports equipment.
stichpunkte: The origin and development of MeiGray
High-profile sales of Michael Jordan and other game-worn items
Equipment from Steph Curry and Conor McDavid
The market outlook and future of game-worn collecting
beschreibung:
Barry Meisel has spent nearly three decades helping transform game-worn memorabilia into one of the most fascinating categories in collecting.
Live from The National, Barry joins Ryan Alford and Brian Ludden to share how he built MeiGray around one fundamental idea: collectors needed a way to prove that the jersey they were buying was actually worn by the athlete. He explains the forensic process behind photo-matching and shares the stories behind a Michael Jordan Finals jersey that sold for $10.091 million and another game-worn relic that reached $24.12 million.
They also discuss counterfeit memorabilia, game-worn relics in trading cards, Steph Curry and Conor McDavid equipment, and why Barry believes authenticated sports memorabilia still has significant room to grow.
Topics Covered
The origin of MeiGray
How photo-matching works
Michael Jordan's $10.091M Finals jersey
The $24.12M game-worn record
Authentication and memorabilia values
Fighting counterfeit memorabilia
Game-worn relic cards
Buying your first game-worn jersey
Steph Curry and Conor McDavid equipment
The future of game-worn collecting
